review: ...and that's a sentence that's probably never been written before.Interstellar is not a movie for everyone. It is a long film and my guess is that many will be asleep by the end of the first hour. It is slow to develop and at times seems like a sequence of university physics lectures on black holes, cosmology, relativity, and quantum physics. Indeed, in order to proceed with the story, it is sometimes necessary to inform the viewer of why what will happen next makes some scientific sense. These lessons are shoehorned in at various points. Scientists themselves may argue over the fine points of some of the physics in the film, but, with a few exceptions, the science is good enough.Now, from what I've just written above, you may think that I would not recommend this picture to anyone. In fact, I would recommend it to everyone. This is because Interstellar is a masterpiece. That's a shaky limb to climb out on, I realize, but even for those who do not like science, there is a payoff. If you like science fiction, you will be satisfied. If you like special effects, you will get them, and, if you like love stories, this, in some ways, is one of the greatest love stories ever written. The idea of the timelessness of love, in all its forms, underpins all the science in this storyand we're back to the wormhole.Despite the high quality of this film, it received no Academy Award nominations for best film and only one minor nomination for best production. This, I believe, shows the shallowness of those involved in selecting these films. Intelligent films have been frequently overlooked in the past. Great films like Inception, The Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, Matrix, Lost in Translation, and even that perennial topper of best films lists, Citizen Kane, never won best picture awards. And remember, Alfred Hitchcock never won an Academy Award for best director.The acting is better than average, but you will not be discussing the quality of the acting when you finish the film. Actually, what you should do is to watch the film again before you reach any conclusions. Anyway, that's what I did. The second time confirmed what I thought. If you look under the scientific veneer of this film, you will see something that will make this, like all great films, timeless. That's just relativity.

review: "Do not go gentle into that good night; Old age should burn and rave at close of day. Rage, rage against the dying of the light."Interstellar was my most anticipated film of the year so my expectations for this film were huge considering the subject matter and the fact that I am a Christopher Nolan fanboy. Despite the several flaws I found with the script, I wasn't disappointed, but I can understand how this might not work for several audiences. First of all the scale of this film was huge even for a Nolan film. He is such a visionary director and he doesn't settle for simple narratives. The script is so complicated at times that it does make you wonder and ask yourself questions about the logic behind the theories. I'm no expert in quantum physics, but I think Nolan does a pretty convincing job of selling it. He did his research along with his brother and they created a solid sci-fi script. Many people complained about the fact that Nolan sometimes explains his plot to the audience instead of just letting them figure it out, but I find it necessary at times because of the complex structure he elaborates for his films. He enjoys creating these puzzles, but at the same time he helps us put the pieces together. Interstellar is one of my favorite films of the year, but I wouldn't rank it amongst Nolan's top 5 best films. If there is someone who can make a film about physics interesting it's Nolan and he manages to do so in this nearly three hour film. This is by far his most ambitious film, but it does fail at being the ultimate space epic film it so desperately tries to be. However there isn't a dull moment in Interstellar and you are never bored by the world he creates. Unfortunately the final payoff of the film isn't as rewarding as I was hoping it to be. The final 20 minutes of the film are perhaps the weakest part of the movie and it sort of tries to wrap everything neatly at the end like most Blockbuster and commercial films try to do.I know I have complained a bit too much about a film I really enjoyed, but I will now try to explain why this is one of my favorite films of the year. First of all the cast in this film is brilliant. There is no better time to cast Matthew McConaughey in a film than now. He had a fantastic 2013 and MUD was my favorite film of that year. He was also amazing in True Detective so I was ecstatic about him joining Nolan's cast for this film. He is great in the lead role and provides some of the most engaging emotional moments of the film. Despite how highly ambitious the subject matter of the film is and how colossal his task, he manages to keep things small by narrowing it all down to the family dynamics (especially through his relationship with his daughter). He is not saving humanity, he is trying to save his daughter. We believe the sacrifice he is making and it is what makes the humanity aspects of this film work. He is going through an inner conflict of accomplishing his purpose by saving humanity while realizing that he has abandoned his children and is missing being a part of that. Jessica Chastain is also great in this film. She is a talented actress and is at a great moment in her career as well. The most emotional scenes of Interstellar revolve around her relationship with her father (McConaughey). There is a scene midway through the film where he receives a message from her in space that is emotionally gripping. Michael Caine and Anne Hathaway team up once again for a Nolan film and deliver despite not having such interesting characters. Casey Affleck, John Lithgow, and Topher Grace were underused, but they are all talented actors. The cast in this film is superb and they lifted this visionary tale even further. But the casting isn't the only element that Nolan gets right. The visuals in this film are fantastic! I was blown away by the scenes that took place in space. The first act of this film is solid and establishes the present world on Earth in a rather realistic way, but the second act raises the film to another level. The scenes in space and the wormhole are amazing. It also becomes suspenseful and full of tension. Unfortunately the third act didn't work as well for me and the ending was a bit too touchy feely. The score in this film by Zimmer was fantastic as usual and helps build the emotion.So in summary the film is incredibly well shot, it has astonishing photography, superb visual effects, an awesome cast and score, and one spectacular robot. The robot in this film has to be one of the best I've seen. He is also the funniest character and helps lighten the serious tone of the film. I loved Interstellar, but if you had issues with the explanation and exposition in Nolan's Inception, than you will have a similar experience with this film because there is a lot of exposition in space about the theories and what it all means. I have no problem whatsoever with this because it is simply part of Nolan's trademark. He wants us to understand every small detail of the plot because he has worked and studied these things before putting them on the script and he doesn't want the audience to miss out on his creative process. Interstellar doesn't get a perfect grade from me because it isn't as epic as it is trying to be, but I will give Nolan a lot of credit for his ambition and for delivering a fun action thriller with huge ideas.

There are things that aren't explained (and would be tough to explain convincingly) and Nolan expertly diverts the viewer to the rest of the story rather than giving a contrived explanation of why things work the way they do.The acting is superb, the characters are believable (not to mention much more human than those in 2001), and overall I would say this is the best science fiction movie I've seen in at least a decade.Is it a better film than 2001? review: Wow. What can be said about Interstellar that hasn't been said before? So I'll just share my thoughts and feelings about this movie. The Nolan brothers have hit yet another home-run with this intergalactic masterpiece. The story is about a single father who's trying to raise his children and provide for them and his father in law. The world is sick, very sick in fact. Cropses are dying and harvests are lost. Farmers have become the world's most important job but soon humanity (or at least a very small part of it) realizes earth can not be saved and that they have to turn to the stars to find salvation.Matthew McConaughey has come a long way since his roles as a piece of man-candy in chick-flicks and he proves it yet again here. He plays his role as Cooper perfectly. The heartache he has to go through while making an impossible choice really pulls you into the story. Saving humanity or seeing his children once more... Anne Hathaway fits the role of Brand well. She's not sexualized as she was in The Dark Knight Rises which gives her the chance to win you over with her acting. And win you over she will! Michael Caine is Michael Caine so you know what to expect there: greatness. Jessica Chastain is wonderful as Murph. She's so strong yet so fragile and it's just heartbreaking to watch her emotional journey. Cassey Affleck takes on the role of Murph's brother and does a great job. There's one more surprise appearance by a big actor which I won't spoil for you. You can already tell the acting jobs are top notch in this picture and they have to be. The story touches on some existential themes which are difficult to comprehend. You have to understand and feel the emotions the characters are going through to grasp the purpose of the story fully.Visually Interstellar impresses. With actual physicists working on the movie you get the most accurate pictures of unearthly events. The visual of black hole Gargantua is actually being used in a scientific publication. The other planets the team visit are equally stunning as they are interesting. Without going in too much detail, the planets feature things we all know but they are portrayed in a way you've never seen before.Now let me take the time to gush over the music in this film. You may think the music isn't as important as the acting or the story but it's with music this good you understand it is actually a character in the movie. The music is gorgeous. It's epic when it needs to be and emotional when the story requires it. I found myself nearly in tears over the music when I didn't expect it. Hans Zimmer proves he can create delicate and fragile pieces of music as well as epic, dark and heavy soundtracks like he has done for The Dark Knight Trilogy.So in summary Interstellar isn't just a space movie. It isn't a science- fiction movie at heart. It's a movie about humanity and about saving it and not just in a literal sense. It's about finding our own humanity. It's about family, it's about love because that is the main theme which drives the characters. It's the core foundation for all their actions and choices. But above all, this film is about hope. It's about believing in ourselves and the power we can muster when we fight for our loved ones.Interstellar is one of the most amazing movies I've ever had the privilege to see. Please, go see this film.

review: This movie is very good. Personally, I think Interstellar truly delivers as Christopher Nolan's best masterpiece. Maybe the general population would put this blockbuster seventh place in the category of the 10 best space movies. I for one would rank it third behind First Man starring Ryan Gosling and Alfonso Cuaron's Gravity respectively.I like Interstellar, because it focuses mainly on personal loss and the love one feels for their family. The beginning is spectacular! I love how it opens with a farm surrounded by crops of corn, a humble beginning. Its much better than starting the movie with all that intense, apocalyptic action we see at the beginning and end of superhero movies.The story plot structure is great as well. Cooper is going into space with a crew to a mission to find a new habitat for the next generation of mankind after the food resource begins to die. But even more so bittersweet, he must say goodbye to his beloved daughter Murph and the rest of his family. As he descends further off into space, time becomes either slower or quicker, and his family starts to age, even though, he's been in space for a brief period of time.Along the way, Cooper makes a lot of good, trusted devoted friends on his mission, including those two hilarious cubicle robots, CASE and TARS (I often confuse one for the other). Its neat when they descend into the black hole and kiss goodbye to their galaxy, because it reminds me of the star gate tunnel in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey and the robots make me think of the monoliths because of their shape. I love the suspense that builds as they land on different planetary terrains.Above all, I like it when Cooper descends into Gargantua's abyss toward the end and finds himself all alone in that 5th dimension, which appears at first as a library of flashbacks. Don't wish to spoil for you guys out there, so best not to read my review. For those of you that have watched Interstellar, I'd like to say how Cooper at first feels depressed and personal emptiness for saying goodbye to his daughter, and the loss is greatly heavy I agree, but soon realizes that the theories she had of a ghost in her bedroom was his presence all along.He then is transcended to a new dimension and awakens to find his daughter Murph as an old lady on her deathbed just like the Professor Brand, surrounded by her friends and family. That moment they share together at the end is just downright touching, for me personally as my grandmother Lois is currently ailing from dementia and staying at a convalescent hospital. Usually, the parent dies before the child, but the irony of the child dying first is another essential characteristic Nolan contributed to in this film. The advice that the old Murph gives Cooper at the end is pure poetry and unforgettable, leaving the audience shedding tears of joy, including myself.So in conclusion, Interstellar delivers generally because its a story about the way we feel for others we love that wouldn't give them up for anything, not even a silly mission that is considered a mandatory task like saving the world from famine or finding a new place for humanity to thrive. Family comes first. And that's what I love of this film.46 people found this helpful.

This sci-fi epic is more than just an adventure across the cosmos; it is a profound meditation on love, sacrifice, and the limits of human potential. With breathtaking cinematography, a mesmerizing score by Hans Zimmer, and a thought-provoking narrative, Interstellar is an unforgettable cinematic experience.A Visual and Auditory MarvelOne of the most striking aspects of Interstellar is its visual spectacle. From the dusty landscapes of Earth to the awe-inspiring vastness of space, every scene is crafted with meticulous attention to detail. The film's depiction of celestial bodies-black holes, wormholes, and distant planets-is not only visually stunning but also scientifically grounded, thanks to the input of physicist Kip Thorne. The use of practical effects combined with CGI creates an immersive world that feels both realistic and otherworldly.Complementing the visuals is Hans Zimmer's hauntingly beautiful score. The music is deeply emotional, evoking a sense of grandeur and loneliness that perfectly matches the film's themes. The use of organs and atmospheric sounds creates an ethereal quality, heightening both the tension and the emotional weight of the story. Zimmer's score is more than just background music-it is an integral part of the film's storytelling.A Story That Balances Science and EmotionInterstellar is a rare sci-fi film that seamlessly blends complex scientific concepts with deeply human emotions. While the narrative explores time dilation, relativity, and the survival of the human race, it never loses sight of its emotional core. At its heart, the film is about relationships-between parents and children, between explorers and their mission, and between humanity and its place in the universe.The screenplay, co-written by Christopher and Jonathan Nolan, takes audiences on a journey filled with twists, moments of awe, and philosophical reflections. The film raises profound questions about destiny, the power of human connection, and what it truly means to explore the unknown. While some of the scientific concepts may seem dense, the film presents them in a way that is accessible without oversimplifying them.A Stellar Cast with Powerful PerformancesThe performances in Interstellar are nothing short of remarkable. Matthew McConaughey delivers one of the best performances of his career, portraying a complex character who is both a determined explorer and a loving parent. His emotional depth and sincerity make the journey all the more compelling.Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, and the rest of the supporting cast also bring their A-game, delivering nuanced performances that add layers to the story. The chemistry between the actors feels genuine, making the emotional beats hit even harder. There are moments of heartbreak, hope, and triumph, all brought to life through stellar performances.A Thought-Provoking ExperienceOne of the greatest strengths of Interstellar is its ability to provoke thought long after the credits roll. The film challenges viewers to contemplate the nature of time, the fragility of human existence, and the unbreakable bonds of love. It is a film that rewards multiple viewings, as each watch uncovers new layers of meaning.That being said, Interstellar is not a conventional sci-fi blockbuster. Its pacing, especially in the first half, is deliberate, taking time to establish its characters and themes. Some audiences might find certain elements abstract or emotionally overwhelming, but for those willing to immerse themselves, the payoff is immense.Final ThoughtsInterstellar is a cinematic masterpiece that pushes the boundaries of what science fiction can achieve. It is a film that is as emotionally moving as it is intellectually stimulating. With breathtaking visuals, a powerful score, and a compelling narrative, Interstellar is an unforgettable journey through space and the human heart.Whether you are a sci-fi enthusiast, a fan of emotional dramas, or simply someone who appreciates great filmmaking, Interstellar is a must-watch. It is not just a film-it is an experience, one that lingers in the mind and soul long after it ends.

review: Interstellar is a movie that is a bit rare these days. Not only for its subject matter; the very cold and philosophical sci-fi perspective, but for the fact it kept itself secret for so long. For the first time in years did a blockbuster come by that wasn't fully spoiled in the trailers. And that pays off in the end.To keep the premise short: Earth is doomed and former-astronaut-turned-farmer Cooper finds himself being an astronaut again after a bit of a too-coincidental event that places him in the middle of a top secret NASA operation. Cooper and crew go through a wormhole and then starts the game of deciding what is more important: saving time to be able to see their families if they make it back, or leave everything behind and colonize one of three potentially habitable planets.An intriguing scenario. Visually Interstellar knocks it out of the park: sterile shots of space and shots harking back to days of crappy stop-motion effects place a very 70's sci-fi mark on the movie. Music is superb and acting in the lead roles is great. In many respects, and this isn't an original remark but still..., this movie is 2001: A Space Odyssee 2.0.And that is also where its flaws stem from. Whereas 2001 had a real philosophical weight to it, I personally never really felt the urgency in Interstellar was truly important. There is some scientific explaining that feels like the 'just throw around some sci-fi slang' trope, which kind of ruins the immersiveness of the otherwise great movie. Many people praised the movie for the emotional weight it carries between Cooper and his daughter. Me? I didn't feel it. As a kid yes, and there is one scene that does to the relation trouble justice. But in the end the thing felt a bit hollow.Maybe that is a side effect of Spielberg's legacy on this movie. Something that is a very positive thing in the rest of the 3 hours you'll watch Interstellar. There are the classic Spielberg shots: kids gazing into the distance, and most of all a great sense of wonder and excitement of going somewhere new. The real Nolan touch comes at the very end when he pulls a bit of an "Inception" and plays with time travel a bit.Overall Interstellar is an absolute joy to watch. A visually strong movie with strong leading roles and an interesting plot. There is little wrong about it...only that in my opinion it has set the bar too high for itself to reach it. It lacks the philosophical weight and emotional urgency it strives for, being a tad hollow in the end.Still: one of the best movies of this year and a definite watch for sure!8/10

review: I've seen a lot of movies, reading IMDb for upwards of a decade without ever writing a review. This film brought me out of lurking.When my wife and I finished Interstellar, we sat talking about it in the car for almost four hours. Everything from the technical film work (editing, camera, lighting) to the acting was impeccable. Without making this an extended review, let's just say that there is something for everyone in this film.For people that want action and excitement, mile high waves and exploring unknown worlds will keep you gripped. For others who want to mull over complex themes and motifs, the film questions what it means to love, what it means to be human, and so much more. For those who want fantastic awe inspiring visuals, Nolan manages to paint his black holes and galaxies with mesmerizing beauty yet he never pushes his frame to the realm of obnoxiously flashy.On the other hand, for people who want to just escape into another world for a few hours, the film will take you right out of your seat and into the stars. For people who want a little touch of love, McConaughey's fatherly love for his daughter came through loud and clear -- while Anne Hathaway had some wonderfully sincere moments of her own.Having said that, I'm sure there are plenty of people who will HATE this movie; just like they hated Inception the first time they saw it. Eventually, I think those people will come to appreciate Interstellar.While the film doesn't have the multilinear story levels of Inception, in my opinion, it's far more complex. Interstellar is a very personal film -- the themes and meaning sown into the story are incredibly complex. The way it portrays reality is likewise complex. The possibilities, conclusions, underpinning spine of the story are all incredibly complex. So complex that certain parts of the film have to be portrayed in a way that will come across as semi-abstract. The visual metaphors of several scenes towards the end of the film will likely alienate simple seeking movie goers.For people that don't enjoy complex film -- this movie is not for you. review: Christopher Nolan's *Interstellar* (2014) is a bold and ambitious science fiction epic that explores themes of love, sacrifice, survival, and the unyielding human desire to explore the unknown. It blends intellectual rigor with emotional depth, combining cutting-edge scientific theories with a deeply personal narrative. Set in a future where Earth is ravaged by environmental collapse, the film follows a team of astronauts who venture beyond our galaxy in search of a new habitable world to ensure the survival of humanity.One of the most remarkable aspects of *Interstellar* is its blending of mind-bending science with human emotion. Nolan, working with physicist Kip Thorne as a scientific consultant, ensures that the film adheres to realistic portrayals of concepts like black holes, wormholes, and time dilation, even as it ventures into speculative territory. The use of theoretical astrophysics adds a unique intellectual layer to the story, making it not only a visually stunning spectacle but also a thought-provoking meditation on space and time.Visually, *Interstellar* is nothing short of spectacular. Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, taking over from Nolan's usual collaborator Wally Pfister, crafts some of the most breathtaking space sequences ever seen on screen. The depiction of Saturn's rings, the alien planets, and the wormhole is awe-inspiring, pushing the boundaries of what is possible in cinematic representation of space. The film's sound design is equally impressive, with Hans Zimmer's score providing an atmospheric and emotionally charged backdrop. The deep, resonant organ music and swelling strings accentuate the film's themes of love and human perseverance, giving the film an almost operatic quality. Zimmer's work here is one of the standout elements, adding a sense of grandeur that elevates the narrative.The performances in *Interstellar* are also outstanding. Matthew McConaughey, fresh off his Oscar-winning role in *Dallas Buyers Club*, delivers a nuanced and emotionally resonant portrayal of Cooper, a former NASA pilot tasked with leading the interstellar mission. His performance is grounded in a deep sense of personal loss and duty, capturing the character's internal conflict as he struggles to balance his commitment to saving humanity with his love for his family. McConaughey's raw emotion, particularly in scenes with his daughter Murph (played by Jessica Chastain in the adult version), forms the heart of the movie, grounding the complex science fiction plot in real human stakes.The supporting cast is also excellent. Anne Hathaway plays Dr. Amelia Brand, a fellow astronaut with her own emotional arc, while the likes of Michael Caine and Matt Damon round out the ensemble. Caine, as Professor Brand, brings his usual gravitas to a pivotal role, while Damon's turn as a stranded astronaut offers a compelling character study in isolation and desperation.At its core, *Interstellar* is a film about the human condition, exploring how love and sacrifice shape our actions, even in the face of impossible odds. Nolan's screenplay does a commendable job of balancing intricate science with an accessible narrative. The film does ask a lot of the audience in terms of attention and interpretation, particularly in the latter stages when the plot takes some ambitious, at times metaphysical, turns. Some may find the complexity of the film overwhelming, while others may appreciate its open-ended nature and philosophical explorations.Despite its occasional moments of exposition-heavy dialogue and its tendency to lean into sentimentality, *Interstellar* remains an enthralling experience. It is a cinematic journey that requires patience, but it rewards that investment with a satisfying, thought-provoking conclusion that lingers long after the credits roll. The film challenges our understanding of time, space, and human relationships, while also telling a deeply personal story about a father's love for his child.In a cinematic landscape often dominated by spectacle, *Interstellar* is a rare, cerebral blockbuster that combines intellectual stimulation with emotional resonance. It isn't a film for everyone, and its ambitious narrative choices may alienate some, but for those willing to engage with its themes and ideas, *Interstellar* offers a profound meditation on the nature of human existence and the pursuit of knowledge. It can certainly be said to be one of the best films of 2014 and was definitely worth the time spent on seeing this picture. The plot was good, the casting was perfect and then (as always with Nolan) there was the suspense ending which really blew my mind.Why did i use that as my title? That's probably one of the best quotes I've heard in my life.The cinematography is mind-blowing and forms a perfect combination with Zimmer's BGM.I don't want to lay all the plot points on the table so this is a small summary.Basically the Earth is ravaged by a disease called Blight which cause the death of crops at an exponential rate such that humans will soon go extinct.Cooper (McConaughy) is a former pilot and now farmer and a father of two.He accidentally stumbles upon NASA who have discovered a wormhole which could lead to other planets that could possibly sustain life.So Cooper is recruited to lead a team to find a new planet where life can continue.After I saw the movie most people were I met were comparing this movie to Kubrick's 2001.I found that really annoying because Kubrick's work is very different from this film. 2001 is more of a visual experience. It is more of an artwork than a movie. The main reason where Nolan wins over the masses is the presence of emotions and feelings which are hardly present in 2001. Most of us want films which can take our feelings and play with it that at the end of the movie we are left crying or happy. Well,let me say that this film does play with our emotions but it also leaves us with something to reflect upon. Some curiosity of the unknown that our human species will always have about intelligent life elsewhere in the universe.Many of my friends told me that they found really hard to understand the ending but somehow i feel different. I'm not saying that the ending was not complex but it is not so difficult to understand if you have at last a basic idea of space and time. Coming back to the movie, the performances of all the actors were exceptional. McConaughy nails it with an enthralling performance which may see him win the Oscar for consecutive years.Mackenzie Foy really impresses and shows amazing potential.All other actors carried out their roles to perfection but these two deserve special mention. TARS, a bot with a comic sense of humor provides enough comedy required for this epic space drama.Also lots of awesome quotes and punchy dialogues which will have the audience applauding uncontrollably(Like I said, we are slave to our emotions and Nolan is the master). At various points in the film I was Happy,sad,curious,tense,relieved,surprised and a lot of other emotions that cant be described on paper.This isn't Nolan's best either if you compare it with The Dark Knight or Inception. Although people argue that Interstellar got a lot wrong about scientific theories,at the end of the day isn't that what sci-fi is all about?Haven't you seen this movie yet? Well, what on Earth are you waiting for? (pun intended)

review: I would first like to say that I thoroughly enjoyed the movie from start to finish. After watching the movie a second time, it was even more enjoyable. This movie had your typical Nolan charm, nuanced dialog that features numerous examples of intelligent foreshadowing and providing answers for questions that are brought up later in the movie. There is a prevailing theme that permeates the entire movie, however I actually missed it the first time I saw the movie because of a bathroom break. It was there throughout the entire movie, but like the last piece of the puzzle, it tied everything together. That's the beauty of Nolan's storytelling, there are so many things that can be discarded as useless, while they actually serve a purpose in the story. When I go into a Nolan movie, I don't expect one thing or another, instead, I watch every scene for what it is and wait for the story to develop in front of my eyes. There were many scenes that I felt were a waste as I first watched the movie, but as the story developed, it became abundantly clear that their role was to serve as an element of good story-telling. After seeing the movie the second time, I was able to pick up on a number of things I missed and the movie does a great job or reconciling most of the "plot holes" that people seem to be complaining about. Again, like other Nolan movies, this movie is not going to be for everyone. If you prefer everything simplified and laid out for you so that even young children could understand, I recommend more of a children's movie or a comic-book movie. If you prefer a bland, almost non-existent story with great visuals, I would recommend a move like Gravity. If you prefer an intelligent story-line with the use of traditional story-telling techniques like foreshadowing, a central theme that permeates the movie in ways you may not fully understand in the first viewing, and that may require you to pay attention in scenes you have yet to understand, I highly recommend Interstellar. If you are someone that likes to nit-pick movies or believes that they are smarter than the movie they are watching and the story-teller who wrote the movie, I would stay away. Chances are you are going to miss key elements of the movie because you won't be viewing the movie for what it is. I have noticed that most of the negative critiques complaining about plot holes actually missed portions of the movies that reconcile those "so-called" plot holes. With all that said, an easy 10/10 and a must see at least twice on IMAX.

review: Interstellar doesn't put a foot wrong, a brilliant 169 minutes covering space, survival and raw human emotion. Hans Zimmer's near-perfect soundtrack is the ideal accompaniment to these epic scenes, adding drama and gravity to every meticulous shot. Equally, the storyline is beyond gripping, a brutally believable tale of a desperate, dying race driven to do anything for survival, balanced against what a father would do for his children.Christopher Nolan's vision of a dying Earth is a stark blend of oranges and greens - crop fields stretching for miles, only to be overwhelmed by the towering dust storms. Leaving Earth, space (and indeed the planets visited) are all equally magical in their own unique ways: Miller's aquatic landscape is eerily bleak, whilst Mann's ice planet is as mind-bending as it is picturesque. Space travel is also done true justice, using wide-angle shots to both convey the vastness of space and the insignificance of man.Matthew McConaughey was practically built for this role, a farmer-turned-engineer trying to juggle saving earth and saving his family; his interactions with Brand (Anne Hathaway) and his daughter Murphy (Jessica Chastain) define the film, testing the strengths of human relationships and their value, even over the distances of space. Credit must also be given to TARS (Bill Irwin), a superbly written, pseudo-sentient robot that becomes as integral a member of the crew as any other.Interstellar is arguably the best sci-fi/space film ever created, superb in every way. The reported scientific accuracy Nolan paid attention to when writing the film is the icing on the cake, allowing the plot to be full lived - unlike anything that has come before.

review: I remember watching Interstellar back in 2014 in a small local theater, and when I heard about the IMAX re-release, I couldn't buy my ticket fast enough. Seeing it again on the biggest screen was simply an overwhelming, transcendent experience. The scale, the sound, the visuals - everything feels so much more alive in IMAX. I was genuinely stunned at how well this film holds up, not just as a blockbuster spectacle but as a deeply human story.It's honestly hard to believe Hans Zimmer didn't win the Oscar for this score. In IMAX, the organ-heavy, hauntingly minimalist soundtrack completely envelops you, adding another dimension to every single scene. It doesn't just accompany the action - it propels it, making every moment feel grand, raw, and charged with emotion. That music is the heartbeat of the film, and in a giant theater, it's almost physically felt.Interstellar remains one of my favorite film of all time because it has everything I want in cinema. Christopher Nolan crafted a masterwork that balances jaw-dropping spectacle with profound emotional weight. The visuals are breathtaking, from alien worlds of frozen clouds to the dizzying beauty of the black hole Gargantua. Every frame is crafted to evoke awe and wonder while also grounding you in the reality of the characters' peril and sacrifice.Matthew McConaughey's performance is absolutely phenomenal. He gives Cooper a rugged warmth and vulnerability that feels painfully real. Watching him grapple with the heartbreak of leaving his children behind - especially during the devastating "message" scene - is almost too much to bear. He embodies the spirit of a man driven by duty but torn apart by love and regret. The ending still leaves me gutted every single time, not just because it's sad, but because it feels honest about the cost of sacrifice, love, and hope.What I love about Interstellar is how unashamedly big it is in both ideas and emotions. It doesn't shy away from exploring complex scientific concepts like relativity, time dilation, gravitational lensing, or quantum physics, yet it never forgets that at its core, this is a story about a father trying desperately to get back to his daughter. That human core keeps it accessible and devastatingly relatable.Watching it again in IMAX reminded me just how technically astonishing this film is. Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography is spectacular, with vast shots that make you feel both insignificant and awestruck. The docking sequence remains one of the most intense, breathtaking scenes I've ever watched in a theater. The use of practical sets and real locations, like Iceland standing in for alien planets, gives it all a tactile authenticity missing in so many effects-heavy films.I also love that Nolan and physicist Kip Thorne went so far as to create scientifically accurate models of black holes, so detailed they actually contributed to academic research. That commitment to realism doesn't just look cool - it gives the entire film a sense of weight and credibility.Some critics have called Interstellar overambitious or emotionally manipulative, but for me that's its greatest strength. It dares to be sincere, to wear its heart on its sleeve, to ask big questions about love, time, sacrifice, and our place in the universe. It's the rare blockbuster that doesn't just want to entertain - it wants you to feel something profound.Seeing it again in IMAX was the perfect reminder of why it's one of my favorite films. It's an experience that makes you feel small in the universe yet deeply connected to what makes us human. Interstellar isn't just a movie - it's cinema at its most ambitious, emotional, and awe-inspiring. A perfect 10/10 for me, every single time.

Nolan's dorkiness is put to good use and the film's best parts do suggest old school hard sci fi novels it is trying so hard to emulate, the visual palate is a bit more vivid and before collapsing under his usual overexplanation some of its scenarios are more intriguing than dour. What escapes Nolan is that what makes something like Randezvous with Rama resonate is not those length scientific explanations and interchangeable overcompetent space professionals but that there is the unknown and the excitement of meeting it for the first time. Interstellar pays lip service to science explorer spirit but like all Nolan films it has no curiosity or imagination, it moves not toward an expansion of the gaze but its entrapment (as every other Nolan film men ultimately is in a trap of his own making even if a more benign one). Nolan's cinema is never about the possibilities of the unknown but about striping it of them.

review: Interstellar is a visually stunning but deeply flawed film that prioritizes emotional spectacle over scientific coherence. Its depiction of time dilation is exaggerated, the concept of love as a fundamental force is unscientific, and the black hole sequence relies on nonsensical pseudo-physics. The film's emotional core feels immature, relying on overwrought sentimentality rather than genuine depth. review: 2001, anyone? That brilliant piece of filmmaking that challenged us to do something that mainstream Hollywood has long since shelved: Think. Use your wonderful brains, people! Remember that films don't have to be simply a means to an end; they can push past our own intellectual limitations, establish beautifully thought-provoking horizons just beyond our reach, and best of all, can be memorable not for what they say, but for what they do. It physically pains me to see promising filmmakers with the appropriate intellectual boundlessness to follow in Kubrick's footsteps pushed to the side in favour of bland individuals with little more than visuals and violence in their creative arsenal. Admittedly, I enjoy my CGI extravaganzas as much as the next guy, and that is why Interstellar is a six-and-a-half-star film in my book. As far as visuals go, it's really, well, stellar. But it is simply too unsatisfying and draws too many parallels with 2001 (without delivering on them) to be considered as anything more.Here's the rundown: Earth is dying. Sandstorms are consuming the world (Mad Max prequel?). Humanity is losing hope. It's all very bleak, but concepts often are. In fact, as far as original settings go, it's rather stirring. The settings in most pre-apocalyptic films are already basically destroyed, but in Interstellar, the bleak atmosphere of impending destruction is done rather well. It invoked within me a surprisingly genuine lack of hope. But this is mostly owing to the fact that this segment of the film was shot in rural Alberta, which is pretty close to where I live, so I was able to recognize the deterioration of the landscape, having been there many times in my childhood.Matthew Mcconaughey stars as Cooper, a retired pilot working on the farm with his son, daughter, and dad. I've always found Mcconaughey's performances to be rather cloying, since the first film I saw him in was Mud and he fit so perfectly into the role that I can't exactly see him doing anything else. Coop's daughter, Murph, finds extraterrestrial messages that send them off to the secret NASA headquarters, which are surprisingly close to their house. Coop meets the head of NASA (Michael Caine) and his daughter (Anne Hathaway). He is then offered the opportunity to leave Earth to find a new home for humanity, which he reluctantly accepts (to the selfish ire of Murph).When the space scenes are actually in space (Saturn, the wormhole, and the black hole), they are undeniably breathtaking. There is a particularly beautiful shot in which the spaceship, little more than a speck in the distance, silently glides past Saturn, kindling a sense of the emptiness, loneliness, and most importantly, sheer vastness of space. But once we step inside the ship, the story and narrative begin to lose their momentum as the actors discuss love, nature, and all sorts of misguided ideas with all the intelligence of, well, actors. The scientific discussions are sort of engaging, but the film would have succeeded just as well had science been left undisturbed.Since we're on the topic of science, let me say this: I don't understand why people revel in Interstellar's scientific accuracy. Films are not textbooks, and if you think they are, you'd probably be better off reading a textbook. You might as well go after The Matrix for being an affront to the laws of physics. And the science in Interstellar is basic stuff. It's thin, easily understood, and easily applied. Notice 2001 had no science. There were no explanations, scientific discussions, nothing. But the question remains: did we need them? Of course not.Anyway, back to Interstellar. After they go through the wormhole (which was put there by unknown sentient beings), they arrive at a solar system orbiting a black hole which has three promising planets. Black holes mess with time, and that concept is played with rather effectively, except for the fact that it turns Murph into an annoyed, peevish Jessica Chastain who takes up too much screen time.And then one of the single most viscous and ridiculous monologues about love takes place. It would have been fine, had Nolan realized that love and science don't mix, and when they do, it just sounds ridiculous. But it happens, and its saccharine sentimentality induces cringes of a ridiculous magnitude. Your reaction to this scene (and perhaps the whole film) is a testimony to your cynicism. Needless to say, this scene made me feel like dung, and when Matt Damon's character sees it fit to do the same thing, I felt even worse. The script is long-winded and pretentious, saying too much when saying less would have a greater effect.However, the docking scene is excellent, a visual marvel among visual marvels, a raucous nod to 2001 that forcefully pushes past Kubrick's weightless spaceship ballet into something that is stunningly intense, but stunningly serene as well.Interstellar's climax is extremely disappointing, a strange mix-up between 2001 and Deus Ex Machina that has the audacity to present itself as profound. Given the buildup of the hopeless "no escape" feeling generated by the first bit of the film, the ending is a blatant narrative cop-out that was hastily strung in when the Nolans realized that they already had way too many pages and had to figure out a way to end it, and fast. Which they do, and the audience is greatly the worse for it.Interstellar is a film trapped by the impossibility of its own concept to find itself at a happy ending, its blandly scripted and acted characters, and its desire to be something more, without having the intellectual horsepower and narrative creativity to do so. Perhaps if Interstellar slimmed itself down by discarding its plot, characters, and dialogue, it could have been a fantastic theoretical documentary that swept us into a stunning unknown.

review:
I've finally gotten around to seeing this latest "Black Christmas" movie. First, it's "Black Christmas" in name only. If you're looking for Billy or phone calls from the moaner, you will be disappointed. I think you have to go into this knowing it's its own movie and not part of Bob Clark's "Black Christmas" storyline.
As stated in many reviews, it is pretty heavy-handed with its messaging. The messaging itself is fine and good. Personally, I prefer subtlety over an in-your-face approach. For instance, I love when actors can convey so much with a look and not require dialog to tell the audience what he/she is thinking. There is no doubt the filmmakers were going to make sure everyone understood the purpose of this film. Even at the end of the movie when the explanation is given for what's going on, I would assume most audience members already had it figured out, so, again, we didn't need a drawn-out explanation for the proceedings.
All that said, I thought the first 70 minutes of the film were great. Although predictable and heavy-handed with the message, I liked the lead characters and cared about them. I thought the actors did a great job, and the movie went along at a nice pace. All the scares have been seen multiple times before, so there wasn't anything scary in the action. The final 20 minutes, after the lead figures out what's going on, is a let-down. I understand its inclusion and drives home the point they are trying to make, but I thought it was a little too much, having me wonder if the filmmakers think I'm too dumb to figure this out. If they wanted something scary, I think they would've needed to keep everything at a human level.
Anyway, overall, I thought the film had a great beginning and progression, but the payoff was lacking with a message too in-your-face where a little subtlety could've made for a better viewing experience.

review: Having previously seen "Date Movie" and "Epic Movie" (also by these gentlemen) and "Plan 9 From Outer Space" (by the equally talented Edward Woodward) I was gasping and sweating and feeling my anus slacken with anticipation when I heard this movie was going to be released. I was even more delighted when I saw the trailer. All too often comedy movie trailers contain all the best jokes, leaving nothing funny for the actual movie. I knew this movie was going to be great when I saw the trailer and there wasn't ONE FUNNY BIT IN IT!!!!! Clearly these were film makers who did not need to advertise their greatness, as they could rely on their genius to advertise itself. I knew we were going to experience a comedy masterpiece on par with "Diff'rent Strokes", "Australia's Funniest Home Videos" or Michael Jackson's cosmetic surgery.I set up camp outside the box office 2 days before tickets went on sale to be sure we got the first tickets accompanied, after a sound thrashing, by my wife and my little boy. For two days and nights we struggled on that lonely sidewalk against hunger and thirst and heat and exposure, and towards the end we had to resort to drinking our own urine. But it was worth it, because when "Meet the Spartans" finally opened we were the only people in the cinema.And what a movie it was! My own memories are a little hazy given the addled state I was in after two days in the street. For my own part, I was laughing and hollering too much at the little purple animals floating around in the cinema to notice much of the movie. I do remember bits of the trailer getting repeated over and over again, but that must have been the hallucinations as well. However I do remember my wife and my little boy found it so funny they were too astonished to laugh. After a while the exertions of the previous 2 days took their toll and they fell asleep with their precious heads lolling into my unwashed groin. But shoot, I wasn't complaining :-) All in all it was probably the greatest day of my life, and perhaps anyone's life.I was delighted to learn that there was a "Meet the Spartans 2". If there was one film crying out for a sequel, it must surely be this one. As with "Weekend at Bernie's", you just got the feeling that one movie was not enough to fully explore the vast richness of ideas on display. One can only hope it will produce more sequels than the Star Wars and the Police Academy series combined.

Spoofed celebrities include Paris with a hunchback, Britney & Lindsey.The war here had less to do with blood and more to do with dance and ‘yo-momma’ stuff! They sure are a drag at some points. Making it worse are gross stuff coming up on screen at regular intervals. Though, just over an hour, you will not feel it was short! This movie is nowhere close to the quality of one of my favorite spoofs, Johnny English (2003), the bond spoof or even the others like the Scary Movie series. Austin Powers would get beyond comparison! To their credit though, the lead characters have really toned up their bodies a-la Leonidas, the Original. A final warning: If you haven’t seen 300, you may easily give this a skip, as most humor will not make much sense!

review: This is the first and probably the best of the 365 dni movies based on a series of popular Polish books. This film follows the story of Laura a wealthy Polish woman who works in the hotel industry and whose live-in-boyfriend takes her to Italy for her 29th birthday. There she is abducted by a young handsome Sicilian mob boss named Mossimo. Five years prior Mossimo's father, who is head of the family, is shot and killed. The bullet that kills his father goes through this heart and into Massimo. Massimo almost dies, but has these visions of a woman who looks identical to Laura...so much so he has had portraits of her made and hung in his home. Flash forward five years and this woman he has been searching for walks out of the airport...and the idea to kidnap her is hatched. He holds her captive telling her he is giving her 365 days to fall in love with him, if she doesn't by her next birthday...he will let her go."It wasn't an offer, it was an order."-MassimoSince his father's death five years ago, Massimo has become the head of his Sicilian Mafia Family. He is your typical alpha male, used to being in control. Laura really knows how to push his buttons."Is that what you call a temper?"In a button pushing incident in Rome, she is the direct cause of getting someone killed and starting a war between two powerful families."I'd like you to teach me to be gentle, for you."-Massimo.To protect Laura, Mossimo sends Laura home to Poland where he has bought her a luxury flat...and the rest you have to watch.This is part one in a series and does end with a cliffhanger. The soundtrack, backdrop, and clothing is phenomenal in this film. There are a lot of criticisms of this film which I want to go on record as saying is entertainment, not a list of what girls want to happen to them...kidnapping and being held hostage by a mobster! This is a fantasy and for what it is...it is great.The actor Michele Morone, who plays Mossimo, is wonderful in the role and I applaud the casting. The actress who plays Laura is also good and I believe well cast...the problem for me is that she is not the most likeable of characters and she is even more unlikeable in the books!There is a fun cameo by the author as "the bride" in this first film.This is a sexy film and a strong recommendation to all fans of dark romance or mafia romance...you will love it!

review: As a HUGE Dragonball fan, I was psyched to the announcement of a live action movie a few months back; but as more information was revealed I started to lose faith. A few days prior to seeing the movie, I had lost all hope of it being remotely good. A 3/10 on IMDb spells disaster. After seeing the movie I can say that I am pleasantly surprised. Although the story was Americanized and modernized to hell and back, it did have its moments of faithfulness to the original manga/anime, specifically with the characters. Goku was very different from the anime, but it was good in its own way. Chatwin did a good job with what he had to work with. I was especially happy with Chow Yun-Fat as Roshi. I was skeptical of his placement in the movie until I saw it myself. He did a fantastic job of bringing the Master Roshi we know to life on the big screen. Lets not forget Yamcha either; he too was able to very faithfully recreate the original character. I was not big on Rossum Bulma but she did do a decent job. Marsters was a good Piccolo but he didn't get as much screen time as I had hope for. As far as anime faithfulness goes, there were several other things throw in that surprised me as far as getting them right but I won't go into detail, I don't want to spoil anything for anyone. Overall, Dragonball Evolution is a decent modern martial arts film with some neat special effects, cool action scenes, but not a faithful adaptation to the series we all know and love. My final verdict is a 6/10 but I could be swayed to a 7/10. Don't let its inaccuracies prevent you from experiencing a new twist on the same old (amazing) story, its still worth your time if you enjoy a good old action movie.

review: On occasion people are wrong about how bad a movie is. Not this time.I grew up on Dragon Ball and Dragon Ball Z. But still if you're going to adapt a series with such a big fan community, you need to keep it's essence.What ruined the movie for me was that Goku's background was raped and transformed him in something he is not. The hero we knew lived alone in the forest with his grandfather and had no contact with civilization, which made him goofy, unadapted to the world and funny. Their characters are aggressively unlikeable, and both actors lean into that discomfort with impressive commitment. It's a credit to the writing and their performances that they are so effective in being grating and unsettling, serving as excellent foils to Pattinson's more grounded and humane presence.The costume design is one of the film's strongest and clearest visual storytellers. Every wardrobe choice is loaded with meaning. These seemingly small touches help paint a larger picture of vanity, control, and rebellion within this dystopian setting. The makeup department deserves equal praise-every character's look is carefully crafted to align with their inner psychology. Whether it's subtle skin blemishes, aged eyes, or pristine, polished perfection, the makeup work ensures each character's design supports who they are at their core.Visually, the film is beautiful. There are several scenes and compositions that would be right at home in a sci-fi artbook. However, while the aesthetic is strong, the cinematography doesn't quite match the ambition of Bong Joon Ho's earlier works. Instead of the dynamic and inventive camera movements seen in films like Parasite or Snowpiercer, Mickey 17 feels more observational. The camera often seems content to simply document the action, rather than actively participate in the storytelling. As a result, it lacks the immersive, artful quality that fans have come to expect from Bong's direction.The score also leaves something to be desired. While it's serviceable and never distracts, it doesn't elevate the film or carve out an identity of its own. For a director known for marrying sound and image with precision, this aspect feels surprisingly muted.All in all, Mickey 17 is an okay film-certainly not bad, and in many ways enjoyable-but perhaps a little disappointing given the pedigree behind it. It's a fun and sometimes thought-provoking ride, bolstered by excellent performances and strong design elements. However, it never fully breaks through into the realm of greatness. If anything, it might suffer most from the burden of expectation. Still, for sci-fi fans and admirers of Pattinson's work, there's enough here to make the journey worthwhile.

review: Director Bong Joon-Ho directs with a certain stylistic confidence that I admire. Usually, it's a little strange like SNOWPIERCER, or it's wonderfully wild and amazing like PARASITE. His latest is a fun combination of the two, a sci-fi dark satire called MICKEY 17 (Don't worry, it's not the 17th installment). Based on the book Mickey7 by Edward Ashton, it tells a story of Mickey (Robert Pattinson), a quiet pushover who ends up in debt to a very bad guy with his extremely lucky friend Timo (Steven Yeun), so he signs up for a colonizing mission on another planet. Not reading the fine print, he signs up to be an expendable, somebody who scientists use as a guinea pig to move science forward. Every time Mickey dies, he gets physically reprinted using a giant 3D printer, then gets his downloaded memories back. The ship is run by an egomaniacal failed politician Kenneth (Mark Ruffalo) and his equally horrible sauce-obsessed wife Ylfa (Toni Collete). They both have some wild scenes and make some acting choices that not everybody will love. I did though. Joon-Ho's work has always had strong social commentary imbedded within, this one being no different. It came across as heavy handed in some ways, but I was having too much fun to care. Pattinson is so good you forget he's playing opposite himself. He has rather great chemistry, with himself. He has grown into a terrific actor. Overall, this feels like seeing a genre-bending uncompromised vision of a great director, but its quirkiness might not be appealing enough for casual audiences. Following up a Best Picture winner like PARASITE must have been tough, but MICKEY 17 is as fun and offbeat as only a Bong Joon-Ho film can be.

I had two main reasons to watch Mickey 17:

The soundtrack was also refreshingly unique-it added an unusual but fitting texture to the sci-fi world.While Parasite and Mickey 17 are vastly different films, they both carry Bong's signature touch of sharp storytelling and genre-blending. I'd call Mickey 17 a sci-fi comedy that balances existential themes with light-hearted chaos.Overall, it's a 10/10 for me. review:
This Movie is very unique in its approach and writing. It feels like it has been made with a vision kept in mind. The script feels majestic and written with a lot of care, executed with great VFX and set design.The Better Part:
The world-building has taken the right amount of time and is done in a way that is easier to understand, making it watchable for a larger audience. It caters well to the audience knowing the Mahabharat Epic. It has VFX which is far greater than any films we have seen in recent times from the Indian cinema. The action sequences are good (especially in the 2nd half) and feel right. Acting done by most of the actors is fabulous. The Acting of Amitabh Bachan stands out the most, making the screen presence of Amitabh Bachan's character feel powerful and grand. While the movies start slowly, they pick up the pace in the second half. The VFX done to show the past of Amitabh Bachan's character is done the right way and feels crisp and realistic. The screenplay is so well written and helps to give the movie a solid base. The movie uses music to elevate already great situations keeping you thrilled. The cameo appearances give you a great feeling while watching the film.The Bad Part:
The film's editing in the first half is a bit too simple and could have been done to take the half to other heights. The dialogue delivery and comic timing of Prabhas's character were not done properly and feels like a forced addition to such a great script. His character feels like a bad attempt at creating Indian Star-Lord. Disha Patni's character feels unnecessary. The Dubbing of various actors does not feel polished in a huge chunk of the film. The villain of this movie is primarily Saswata Chatterjee. Still, even after hiring such a fine actor, the screen presence of his character feels very ordinary and straight out of a Pixar movie.In the end, the movie is flawed but its better part reflects more which helps it to become a good movie. I feel that if you want to experience it with family and friends and have a great time, it is a good recommendation.

review: The movie uniquely blends Indian mythology with dystopian science fiction. I went to the movie with very low expectations, since I had heard a few negative reviews. But boy!...was I surprised. The movie is really good and I thoroughly relished it. I was always a sucker for sci-fi, so the futuristic CGI and visuals were indeed appealing. But more than that, the fact that I had cut my teeth on Indian mythology by voraciously reading the Mahabharata multiple times.....played a pivotal role in my admiration for the film.Seeing my childhood mythological heroes such as Krishna, Arjuna, Ashwathama and Karna come to life on the big screen in a different context was extremely gratifying. You feel transported to a parallel universe and the 'past' amalgamating with the 'future'.Amitabh Bachchan was electrifying in his role as Ashwathama and played a key role in the movie. Prabhas also performed well, but could have delivered more. I still think 'Bahubali' was his best till date. The legendary star Kamal Hassan played the antagonist in an extremely compelling manner. I assume his role will get amplified in the sequel.The only criticism for the movie is that the movie director and story writer have blatantly copied concepts and scenes from almost all major Hollywood sci-fi movies. The dystopian world setup is heavily plagiarised from the epic movie 'Alita - Battle Angel'. The entry scene of Prabhas is from the movie 'Ready Player One'. The sand dunes and desert cinematography is a duplicate of scenes from the movies 'Dune' and 'Star Wars'. Many of the fight scenes were exactly copied from the 'Avengers' and the 'Black Panther' movies. No doubt that the director and the CGI team did an excellent job on the visuals, but there is not a single CGI scene where you don't feel Deja-vu. This I feel is the 'Achilles heel' of the movie which prevents it from ever being considered as a visionary and path breaking film. But the juxtaposition of the Mahabharata characters with sci-fi contextual setting is indeed unparalleled.Final verdict - This is not Adipurush 2...in fact, this is miles away from Adipurush. The CGI is world class, but heavily plagiarised and suffers from lack of ingenuity. If you love sci-fi and action movies, then there is a high probability that you would enjoy the movie. If you also love Hindu mythology, then it would be a bumper extravaganza!

review: I feel like our 12 year old really liked the movie. It has sufficient action and enough catchy tunes to keep him interested and the cuts to our friends from the original for humor seemed to work for him.Visually, the movie was great. I'm not sure this is really a big step up over the current state of animation. A story about talking animals doesn't necessarily benefit or need such photo-realistic animation. We're buying into talking animals so even the quality of the original Lion King would be fine. And if the tradeoff were a much better story but not as visually stunning, I would take that deal all day long.For the adults it was a bit more of a mixed bag. There really was no need to keep going back to the "present" and remind us this was a prequel. At some point, that just felt like they had a run time goal and so added these segments to get there. Just as one would get sucked into the actual story of the movie you would be yanked back for some one-liners and other things that really did nothing to move the story along.Maybe that's because the story itself was not so great overall. I know some took issue with the music, but that wasn't so much the issue for me as just a feel like I was always waiting for something to happen and yet there we were still just wandering the savannah towards Eden. It was mildly interesting to see the origins of key characters, but these are lions so that story is not all that different than what happened in the original movie, it just happened to different animals.Our family had seen Wicked recently and the adults felt the story, music and everything was much better in that movie than this one. Not that this is so bad, but with all the build up perhaps we just were expecting to be wowed by more than the visual effects.

review: I had such an amazing time watching this movie! I understand some of the criticism in other reviews but for me they took nothing away from my huge enjoyment of every minute of this movie. Loved the deep hippie wisdom of Rafiki and Taka's mother. Loved the complicated relationship of the brothers, the foreshadowing, and strangely also enjoyed the heartbreaking realization that a bitter end has already been written for this sweet, sweet beginning. It was challenging my optimistic hope that things will always turn out fine and making me accept sometimes they don't in a way I didn't expect from this movie. Loved the light hearted humor, the score and the breathtaking visuals. And the cuteness overload that were the baby lions. My watch party found the movie moving and emotional and there was repeated crying even by the usually hardened watchers.It's true the movie went quite hard on giving a backstory to everything, but I am such a hardcore Lion King fan, I just found it epic and deeply satisfying.I agree with others that the musical songs were not as iconic and memorable as in the first movie, but that would have been a cherry on top I didn't need for great enjoyment.Inclusion of the comic relief Timon & Pumbaa was great and I would have missed them if they weren't involved. I enjoyed the tie to the continued story in the future and was very happy to get every minute of the runtime.Story-wise the only thing I missed were more meaningful talks among Mufasa & co. About their feelings for each other that could have resolved the plot-driving tension better, but then again these are teenagers or very young adults so an immature way of handling relationships is on point. I did find the choice strange to have Mufasa be the perfect can-do-no-wrong hero the whole time and then fail in the final crucial moment of forgiveness, a failure to show more grace that will ultimately cost his life. But I still found it a strong enough backstory.Overall, a stunning, moving, entertaining movie that I enjoyed greatly. Oh, and I want a baby lion now.

review: I'm hoping Disney takes note. The story is fantastic, very compelling. At the beginning of the movie I was wondering how these two cubs who absolutely loved each other would turn out to be each other's nemeses and the movie delivered (no spoilers). No complaints there. I also liked the overall ark and how it all ties together, with the Outsiders later making a reappearance in Simba's Pride with Kovu and all that (I presume). Taka's character ark was really good.That's all great... and then there was the script. So many things could have been improved with a bit of simple writer editing, it's gotta be the easiest part of creating a movie, and unfortunately the script is kinda what makes or breaks a movie. The conversations were very clunky, some lines were just cringe, and character interactions were too artificial. Too much telling and not showing (the cons of CGI? Too hard to do this?). Two examples stand out: at the beginning, when Mufasa's parents talk about how barren things are around them... but their suffering is barely shown. They actually seem to have it pretty good in the desert. There are lots of animals there, and random pools of water. Next, there was literally no reason for giraffes, buffalos and elephants to join Mufasa's fight. The ONLY way to make that compelling, and to make Mufasa a compelling king of ALL animals, was to have him accumulate way more friends along the way than just Rafiki, Sarabi and Zazu. The other animals joining the fight, and then them acknowledging him as king, just wasn't compelling and felt forced. We are *told* they choose him but we are not shown how or why. There were other instances where the story was good but the script was bad, like when Taka's dad instills toxic shame in his son, but the lines to deliver that were way too generic. How about subtle looks, vague hints, teasing and mocking in front of the other males. Don't just spell it out with "this info must never get out, for it is shameful"!Another aspect of the script that didn't work was Rafiki's background. After Simba was an outcast, Timon and Pumbaa were outcasts, and Mufasa was an outcast, Rafiki should not have been a random outcast living among baboons who then banish him. Come on! Just make him a sage, trained by other mandrils to be a sage, who are as cookey as he is and send him on the quest to find Pride Rock (NOT Milele, as that's never mentioned in the original). You can't just have the same story over and over.The great thing about the original was that the songs were standalones, it didn't matter what was going on in the cartoon, you could still hum them. But the songs are too plot-specific, like the "on our way" song jumps from one character singing "I am doing this right now in a plot important way" to another character singing "I am feeling like this right now in a plot important way" so there's no way to listen to them outside of the movie. Like, in the original, Simba sings, "no one saying do this, no one saying be there... free to run around all day, free to do it all my way" etc. And not "I'm gonna ditch Zazu this way, we're gonna get to the elephant graveyard, yay"Finally, and this one hurt me the most, was the science flaws. This is Africa. Mount Kilimanjaro is the ONLY mountain with snow on it and it is not a mountain range, it is one, singular, conically shaped volcano. Newborn lions are not out and about walking, they have their eyes closed, only crawl, and mom hides them in a den. And several other little flaws. The great thing about the original was that they did the research on the geography. Mufasa's death was in the Olduvai Gorge, Pride Rock was one of hundreds of ancient mountain cores across the landscape, Simba runs off into the Ngorongoro highlands, everything is in the Great African Rift Valley. Where are Mufasa and co. Finding the Himalayas??

review:
As a lifelong admirer of The Lion King franchise, I feel compelled to express my deep disappointment with the recent Mufasa prequel and The Lion King remake. These films, which once held such profound emotional depth and storytelling, have sadly been reduced to hollow shadows of their former selves. I hope this letter conveys the gravity of the missed opportunity and the detrimental impact these changes have had on a beloved franchise. I will highlight this in the following points:Simba's Hopeful Scepticism:
One of the most crucial aspects of the original films was their ability to convey emotion through the characters' faces. This emotional connection allowed audiences to deeply empathize with the characters' journeys. For example, when Simba blames himself for his father's death, and Rafiki reveals that his father is still alive, we witness Simba following Rafiki through the woods. In this masterpiece of silent storytelling, we see Simba express a mix of hope, uncertainty, doubt, and eventual realisation. The audience is drawn into his emotional journey, sharing his internal questions-"Is it true?" "Could it be possible?" "Is monkey mad?"-all conveyed through his facial expressions and the evocative background music. This profound emotional depth was missing entirely in the remake leaving viewers disconnected from Simba's internal struggle.Scar's Sarcasm:
In the original The Lion King, Scar's character was defined by his sharp wit, sarcasm, and a sense of cunning that made him one of Disney's most iconic villains. His sardonic line, "Oo, I shall practice my curtsey," accompanied by sly hand gestures and a sneering tone, was a masterclass in delivering disconnect and disregard. Every movement was carefully crafted to reveal his deceitful nature-his resentment towards Mufasa, his jealousy of Simba, and his dangerous ambition.Scar's personality was multifaceted; he wasn't just a villain, but a character with depth. His sarcasm wasn't merely for humour-it was a tool that highlighted his intelligence, his ability to manipulate, and his deep-seated bitterness. This made Scar a memorable and complex antagonist who left a lasting impression on audiences.In stark contrast, the remake completely missed these nuances. Scar's wit and sarcasm were dulled, reducing him to a one-dimensional character lacking the charm and intelligence that made him compelling. The absence of these defining traits stripped away the layers of his personality, leaving a hollow version of the once-vibrant character.Mufasa's Prequel Missteps:Scar's ultimate goal of murdering both his brother Mufasa and his baby nephew Simba in the original The Lion King speaks to a deeply personal and profound betrayal. His act of betrayal isn't born out of mere ambition; it stems from a long history of pain, resentment, and perceived injustice within their familial bond.The decision in the remake to frame Scar's hatred of Mufasa as being motivated by a rejected romantic interest in Sarabi significantly undermines this complexity. Scar's resentment is about more than just losing out on love-that's what makes his betrayal so powerful and heartbreaking. His hate for Mufasa and Simba must have stemmed from something deeper- perhaps the loss of his own wife and child? By making Scar's grudge about a love triangle, the remake strips away all that emotional depth. It turns Scar into a character who's acting out of petty jealousy rather than deep-seated pain.Furthermore, the decision to prioritize casting based on race rather than talent has diluted the essence of these iconic characters. The original Lion King thrived because of its authentic and deeply resonant performances, something sorely lacking in the remake.The original The Lion King is more than just an animated film; it's a profound exploration of love, loss, faith, and the importance of confronting one's past. Through the bond between Simba and Mufasa, we learn that love endures beyond loss, while Mufasa's death teaches Simba-and the audience-about grief and the power of redemption. Simba's journey is one of self-discovery, where he learns that running from the past only delays true healing. The film's spiritual heart lies in the "Circle of Life," a powerful symbol of the interconnectedness of all beings, emphasizing that life's challenges and losses are part of a greater cycle of renewal and growth. This message of embracing life's ups and downs, learning from mistakes, and fulfilling one's role in the grand tapestry of existence resonates deeply. Sadly, the remakes strip away much of this emotional and philosophical richness, replacing it with visual realism that lacks the soul and depth of the original.I urge Disney to consider the disappointment felt by fans and to take meaningful steps towards rectifying these mistakes. A remake guided by those who genuinely understand and cherish the original films could restore the magic that has been lost.

review: The first Old Guard film was a breath of fresh air - original, soulful, and driven by a sense of ancient purpose. While not perfect, it carried emotional weight, and the bond between Andy and her crew felt earned. It ended on a chilling, powerful note: Quinn alive after centuries of torment, setting up what could have been one of the great emotional reckonings in immortal cinema.That moment promised a deep, personal, and mythical sequel. Instead of following through on its promise, it plays it safe, corporate, and shallow - a betrayal of what made the original special.
